title: Lavash
subtitle: The large, thin Armenian flatbread baked on a very hot surface until blistered
excerpt: Lavash is rolled paper-thin and baked in seconds on a scorching surface. The blisters and slight char are what make it. At home, a preheated baking tray or pizza stone under the top element comes close to the intense heat of a traditional clay tonir. Eaten fresh it is pliable; left for a day it crisps into a cracker.
sourceNotes: Lavash is a UNESCO-inscribed traditional bread of Armenia and is eaten across the Caucasus and Middle East. The technique of rolling extremely thin and baking on a high-heat clay surface (tonir) has been documented in culinary literature since at least the nineteenth century. The home oven method described here approximates the high heat using maximum oven temperature and a preheated stone or heavy tray.

recipe.batchNotes: Roll and bake one sheet at a time. The dough keeps well covered for up to 2 hours at room temperature.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soft lavash is best eaten within an hour of baking. To make crisp lavash ahead, leave baked sheets uncovered at room temperature overnight.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Maximum oven temperature (fan or conventional). Preheat a pizza stone or heavy baking tray for at least 30 minutes before baking.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly baked lavash left uncovered at room temperature for 24 hours until it crisps completely. Dried lavash keeps for months, can be broken into pieces and eaten like a cracker, and can be softened again by wrapping in a damp cloth for 10 minutes.

content.text: Lavash is unleavened and requires no proving time. The work is in the rolling: each sheet goes to about 1 to 2 mm, thin enough to see a hand through when held to the light. Rolled too thick, it bakes like a pitta rather than blistering on the surface. Once baked, it can be eaten immediately as a soft wrap, or left out overnight to dry into crisp
Combine the flour and salt in a bowl. Add the warm water and olive oil. Mix until a dough forms, then turn out and knead for 5 minutes until smooth. The dough should feel firm but not stiff.
Divide into 4 to 6 equal pieces. Cover with a clean cloth and rest for 30 minutes. Preheat the oven to maximum heat (240 to 260 degrees Celsius) with a pizza stone or heavy baking tray inside.

On a lightly floured surface, roll one piece of dough as thin as possible, working from the centre outward. Rotate the sheet as you roll. Aim for 1 to 2 mm thickness; it will shrink slightly when placed on the stone.
Scatter sesame seeds over the surface if using, and press them in lightly with the rolling pin.
Carefully transfer the sheet onto the hot stone or tray. Bake for 2 to 4 minutes until the surface blisters and takes on light brown patches. Watch closely; it can catch in seconds.
Remove and cool on a rack. Roll and bake the remaining pieces while the oven stays at maximum heat.

Roll the lavash onto the rolling pin like a scroll to transfer it to the oven. Unroll it directly onto the hot stone without stretching. Alternatively, roll it on a piece of baking paper and slide the paper and dough together onto the stone.
